usage: 그렇게 (like that) + 생각하다 is the everyday way to agree with an opinion.
생각해 보다 = think and see, i.e. mull it over before deciding.
I'll think about it once more.
A soft, polite way to decline or delay without saying no outright.
Here 생각 is a noun (your-thought); 생각하다 unpacks into 생각(을) 하다.
examples: 뭐 생각해?
What are you thinking about?
Casual 해; drop the object and Koreans understand 'about what'.
저는 이 영화가 재미있다고 생각해요.
I think this movie is fun.
To report an opinion, attach -다고 to the plain form (재미있다 → 재미있다고).
가족을 생각하면 힘이 나요.
When I think of my family, I get strength.
생각하면 (when/if I think) + emotion — thinking 'of' a person, not just an idea.
nuance: 생각하다 (a native verb 생각 'thought' + 하다, not Sino-Korean) covers two jobs English splits apart: holding an opinion ('I think it's good') and mentally pondering or picturing ('I'm thinking about it / about you'). The near-synonym 믿다 means to believe with conviction, and 알다 means to know as fact; 생각하다 stays softer and more subjective, so use it for personal views. To report what you think, the partner pattern is -다고 생각하다 (좋다고 생각해요 = I think it's good); this is THE pitfall — English speakers say 생각해요 그것은 좋다 word-for-word, but Korean must embed the clause with -다고 before 생각하다. As a 하다 verb it splits in the negative (생각 안 해요, 생각 못 해요), and the polite stem is 생각해요, never 생각하어요.

mistakes: Saying '생각해요 이거 좋다' to mean 'I think this is good.' Korean needs the quoted clause first: 이거 좋다고 생각해요. The -다고 ending is what carries 'that…'.
Using 알다 (know) for an opinion, as in '좋은 영화라고 알아요.' 알다 is for facts you know; for a view use 생각하다 → 좋은 영화라고 생각해요.
Forming the negative as '안 생각해요.' Because 생각하다 is noun+하다, the 안 goes inside: 생각 안 해요.

usage: Emotion-noun + 을/를 + 느끼다; the feeling is the object, not an adjective.
느끼다 also senses non-emotional things like a difference or a change.
느껴 보다 = experience it for yourself; very common with 분위기.
Turns an adjective (피곤하다) into a noun (피곤함) so 느끼다 can take it.
examples: 추워?
Are you cold? (lit. do you feel cold?)
For bodily cold/hot Korean uses the adjective 춥다, NOT 느끼다 — a key boundary.
그 말에 감동을 느꼈어요.
I was moved by those words (lit. felt being moved).
Past 느꼈어요; 감동을 느끼다 is a set collocation for being touched.
저는 한국에서 정을 많이 느껴요.
I feel a lot of warmth/connection in Korea.
정 is an untranslatable Korean affection; 정을 느끼다 is how you say you sense it.
nuance: 느끼다 (a native verb, no 한자) means to become aware of something through the senses or the heart — an emotion (행복을 느끼다), a physical sensation (통증을 느끼다 = feel pain), or an abstract impression (차이·분위기를 느끼다). The contrast with 생각하다 is sharp: 느끼다 is what your body and heart register, 생각하다 is what your mind concludes. The big English-speaker pitfall is over-using it for states: 'I feel cold/sick/tired' in natural Korean is usually the plain adjective — 추워요, 아파요, 피곤해요 — not 추움을 느껴요. Reserve 느끼다 for when you're consciously naming the sensation as an object (감동을 느끼다, 책임감을 느끼다). Conjugation: the stem 느끼 + -어 contracts to 느껴 (느껴요, 느꼈어요), never the spelled-out 느끼어요.

Writing 느끼어요 / 느끼었어요. The vowel stem contracts: 느껴요 / 느꼈어요.
Using 느끼다 for 'I feel that we should go.' That sense of 'feel = opinion' is 생각하다 in Korean: 가야 한다고 생각해요, not 느껴요.

usage: Person + 을/를 + 기억하다 to ask if someone recalls you.
Object of memory takes 을/를; 기억하다 holds it in the mind.
똑똑히/생생히 기억하다 = remember vividly; a natural intensity adverb.
It doesn't come to me / I can't recall.
Idiom 기억이 나다 (memory arises) is how Koreans actually say 'I (can't) recall.'
examples: 내 생일 기억해?
Do you remember my birthday?
Casual 기억해; a common little relationship test.
그 날을 아직도 기억해요.
I still remember that day.
아직도 (still) + 기억하다 for a memory that lasts.
약속을 꼭 기억해 주세요.
Please be sure to remember the appointment.
기억해 주세요 asks someone to keep it in mind for your sake.
nuance: 기억하다 comes from the 한자 記憶 (記 'record' + 憶 'recollect'), literally 'record-and-recollect,' so it spans both keeping something in memory and calling it back up. The crucial contrast is with 외우다: 외우다 means to memorize by effort (study a list, learn lines), while 기억하다 is simply having or retrieving a memory — you 외우다 a phone number so you can later 기억하다 it. Its opposite is 잊다 (forget). A very natural alternative for spontaneous recall is the idiom 기억이 나다 ('a memory arises'): Koreans say 기억이 안 나요 far more than 기억 못 해요 for 'I can't recall it right now.' Pitfall for English speakers: don't use 기억하다 where English 'memorize' is meant (cramming for a test is 외우다), and remember it's a 하다 verb, so the negative is 기억 안 해요 / 기억 못 해요, with 안 inside.

Saying '기억 못 해요' for a name that just slipped your mind. Native speakers prefer the idiom 기억이 안 나요 ('it won't come to me') in that moment.
Confusing it with 생각나다. 생각나다 = something pops into mind / I just thought of it; 기억하다 = I hold it in memory. They overlap but aren't interchangeable in writing.

usage: Information + 을/를 + 잊다 when a fact drops out of memory.
잊지 마세요 is the standard 'don't forget' reminder.
잊어버리다 adds finality — it's gone for good, often with regret.
못 잊다 = unable to forget; a staple of K-ballads about lost love.
examples: 또 잊었어!
I forgot again!
Casual past 잊었어; 또 (again) admits a habit.
나쁜 기억은 빨리 잊고 싶어요.
I want to forget bad memories quickly.
잊고 싶다 expresses the wish to let something go.
우산을 가게에 두고 그냥 잊어버렸어요.
I left my umbrella at the shop and just forgot about it.
두고 (leave behind) + 잊어버리다 — the umbrella stayed AND slipped my mind.
nuance: 잊다 (native verb) means something disappears from your memory — a password, a promise, a person. Its dead-opposite is 기억하다. The number-one English-speaker trap is the look-alike 잃다 'to lose (a physical object)': you 잃다 your wallet but 잊다 your password. They even sound close (잊다 [읻따] vs 잃다 [일타]), yet swapping them changes the meaning entirely. Koreans very often attach the auxiliary -어버리다 to make 잊어버리다, which adds a nuance of 'it's completely, irretrievably gone,' frequently with a tinge of relief or regret (다 잊어버렸어요). Note the consonant stem conjugates plainly: 잊어요, 잊었어요, and the formal is 잊습니다. For 'don't forget,' the fixed warning form is 잊지 마세요.

Saying 'I forgot my umbrella at the shop' as 우산을 잊었어요 only. If you physically left it behind, Koreans say 우산을 (가게에) 두고 왔어요 or add 잊어버렸어요 — 잊다 alone covers the mind, not the leaving.
Treating 잊어버리다 as a separate, harder word. It's just 잊다 + -어버리다; use it freely for 'totally forgot.'

usage: Thing chosen takes 을/를; 결정하다 = settle the matter.
Please decide slowly / take your time deciding.
천천히 + 결정하다 to reassure someone not to rush.
To decide TO DO something: verb + -기로 결정하다 (가다 → 가기로).
Idiom 결정을 내리다 (hand down a decision) — weighty, like a verdict.
examples: 뭐 먹을지 결정했어?
Did you decide what to eat?
Casual; -ㄹ지 (what/whether) embeds the open question before 결정하다.
여행 날짜를 아직 결정 못 했어요.
I still can't decide the travel date.
결정 못 하다 = unable to settle on it; 못 sits inside the 하다 verb.
회사를 그만두기로 결정했어요.
I decided to quit the company.
Big life choice with -기로 결정하다; this is where 결정하다 outshines 정하다.
nuance: 결정하다 is built on the 한자 決定 (決 'resolve, cut through' + 定 'fix, settle'), so it literally means 'cut through and settle' — reaching a firm choice after deliberation. Three near-synonyms divide the space: 정하다 is the everyday, lighter 'set/decide' (그냥 정해요 = let's just settle it); 선택하다 (選擇) is 'select' from given options; 고르다 is the casual 'pick' (고르다 a fruit, a color). Use 결정하다 for consequential, considered decisions (a job, a move, a date) — for which thing to pick off a shelf, 고르다 or 선택하다 fits better. To decide to DO an action, the partner pattern is -기로 결정하다 (가기로 결정했어요); English speakers often forget the -기로 and say 결정했어요 가다. As a 하다 verb the negative splits: 결정 안 해요, 결정 못 해요. The heavier idiom 결정을 내리다 frames it as 'handing down' a decision.

Forgetting -기로 when deciding to do something: '결정했어요 한국에 가다' is ungrammatical. Embed it: 한국에 가기로 결정했어요.
Forming the negative as 안 결정해요. Inside the 하다 verb: 결정 안 해요 (or 아직 결정 못 했어요 for 'haven't decided yet').

usage: Meal + 을/를 + 준비하다; getting food ready.
Note: the exam takes 을/를, NOT 'for' — 시험을 준비하다, not 시험에.
I braced myself (lit. prepared my heart).
마음의 준비 = mental/emotional readiness; a fixed phrase.
Passive 준비되다 = to be ready; the natural reply to 'are you ready?'
examples: 밥 준비했어?
Did you get the food ready?
Casual; 밥 stands in for 'a meal' generally.
내일 발표를 준비해야 해요.
I have to prepare for tomorrow's presentation.
준비해야 하다 expresses the obligation to get ready.
선물을 미리 준비해 두세요.
Prepare the gift in advance (and keep it ready).
준비해 두다 = prepare and leave set; 미리 reinforces 'ahead of time.'
nuance: 준비하다 comes from 한자 準備 (準 'standard, level' + 備 'provide, equip'), literally 'get equipped to standard' — to ready things or yourself beforehand. It naturally collocates with events and outcomes: 시험을 준비하다, 여행을 준비하다, 저녁을 준비하다, 마음의 준비. Compare 마련하다 ('arrange/procure' funds or a place — 집을 마련하다) and 챙기다 ('gather up, pack' your own belongings — 여권 챙겼어? = did you grab your passport?); 준비하다 is the broad 'prepare,' while 챙기다 zooms in on not forgetting items. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'prepare FOR the exam' tempts 시험에 준비하다, but Korean treats the exam as a direct object — 시험을 준비하다. Also don't reach for 만들다 'make' when you only mean getting ready. As a 하다 verb, negate inside (준비 안 해요), and its passive 준비되다 ('be ready') is everywhere: 준비됐어요.

usage: Time + 에 + 운동하다 for a routine.
I worked out at the gym.
헬스장 (gym) + 에서; the place where exercise happens.
운동 is also a noun: 운동(을) 하다, 운동을 시작하다.
I don't get enough exercise (lit. it's exercise-shortage).
운동 부족 — a common health complaint built on the noun 운동.
examples: 요즘 운동해?
Are you working out these days?
Casual check-in; 요즘 (lately) frames an ongoing habit.
건강을 위해서 운동하고 싶어요.
I want to exercise for my health.
건강을 위해서 (for the sake of health) + 운동하고 싶다.
요즘 바빠서 운동 못 해요.
I can't exercise these days because I'm busy.
Negative ability 운동 못 하다, with 못 inside the 하다 verb.
nuance: 운동하다 = 한자 運動 (運 'move, transport' + 動 'move') + 하다, literally 'movement-movement,' i.e. to physically exercise. The same noun 운동 also means a sports movement or a social campaign, but with 하다 it's working out. A key feature for learners: Korean builds most sports the same way — noun + 하다 (축구하다 play soccer, 수영하다 swim), though racket sports take 치다 'hit' instead (테니스 치다). The contrast with 놀다 ('play, hang out, have fun') matters: 놀다 is unstructured fun, 운동하다 is purposeful physical activity, so don't say 놀다 when you mean training. Natural collocations: 헬스장에서 운동하다, 건강을 위해 운동하다, 운동 부족. As a 하다 verb the negatives split — 운동 안 해요, 운동 못 해요 — and you can swap in 운동을 안 하다 with the object marker for a touch more emphasis.

usage: Tool + 을/를 + 사용하다; the thing used is the object.
Common with payment methods: 카드/현금을 사용하다.
사용 중 (mid-use) — the sign and phrase for a busy restroom or machine.
Please tell me how to use it.
사용법 (use-method) = instructions; built on the noun 사용.
examples: 이거 써도 돼?
Can I use this?
Very casual — here Koreans naturally swap in 쓰다, the everyday twin of 사용하다.
여기서 와이파이를 사용할 수 있어요.
You can use the wifi here.
사용할 수 있다 states availability or permission.
이 화장실을 사용해도 돼요?
May I use this restroom?
-아도 돼요? asks permission; 사용하다 is polite and neutral for facilities.
nuance: 사용하다 is the 한자 使用 (使 'employ, make use of' + 用 'use') + 하다 — to put a tool, service, or facility to use. Its everyday native twin is 쓰다, which means the exact same 'use' but sounds more casual and conversational (이거 써도 돼? vs the more formal 이거 사용해도 돼요?). A third relative, 이용하다 (利用), leans toward using a service or system (지하철을 이용하다 = use the subway, 시설을 이용하다 = use the facilities). Rule of thumb: speech and casual notes → 쓰다; signs, manuals, and polite requests → 사용하다; services and transport → 이용하다. The pitfall is over-formalizing chat: a friend asks to borrow your pen and 사용해도 돼? sounds stiff — say 써도 돼? Also beware that 쓰다 is a homonym meaning 'write' and 'wear (on the head/face),' so context disambiguates. As a 하다 verb, negate inside: 사용 안 해요, 사용 못 해요.

structuredNuance.t: 사용하다 means to put a tool, service, or facility to use.

Its everyday native twin is 쓰다, which means the exact same 'use' but sounds more casual and conversational (이거 써도 돼? vs the more formal 이거 사용해도 돼요?). A third relative, 이용하다 (利用), leans toward using a service or system (지하철을 이용하다 = use the subway, 시설을 이용하다 = use the facilities). Beware that 쓰다 is a homonym meaning 'write' and 'wear (on the head/face),' so context disambiguates.
한자 使用 (使 'employ, make use of' + 用 'use') + 하다.
As a 하다 verb, negate inside: 사용 안 해요, 사용 못 해요.

mistakes: Using formal 사용하다 in casual speech where 쓰다 fits: 'can I use this?' to a friend is 이거 써도 돼?, not the stiff 이거 사용해도 돼?
Using 입다 (wear clothes) for 'use': you don't 입다 an app or a card. Tools and services take 사용하다/쓰다.
Saying 안 사용해요. Inside the 하다 verb: 사용 안 해요. And for transport/services, 이용하다 often sounds more idiomatic (버스를 이용해요).

usage: 혼자 (alone) + 여행하다 to describe travel style.
Place + 을/를 + 여행하다 = tour that place.
I want to go on a trip.
여행(을) 가다 — the most common everyday way to say 'go traveling.'
Compound 배낭여행 (backpack-travel) + 하다; 여행 is a flexible noun.
examples: 방학 때 어디 여행해?
Where are you traveling during the break?
Casual; 어디 (where) + 여행하다.
내년에 유럽으로 여행 갈 거예요.
I'll travel to Europe next year.
Destination + 으로 + 여행(을) 가다 — the go-to natural pattern.
기차로 여행하는 걸 좋아해요.
I like traveling by train.
Means of transport + 로/으로; 여행하는 걸 좋아하다 states a preference.
nuance: 여행하다 is 한자 旅行 (旅 'journey, sojourn' + 行 'go') + 하다 — to travel, typically for leisure or sightseeing. Here's the natural-usage point most textbooks bury: Koreans far more often say 여행(을) 가다 'go on a trip' or 여행(을) 하다 with the noun split out than the bare verb 여행하다. A destination then takes 으로/로 ('toward') in 부산으로 여행 가다, or 을/를 when you 여행하다 a place you tour around (유럽을 여행하다). Compare 관광하다 (觀光, 'sightsee' — the tourist act of viewing attractions) and plain 가다 'go'; 여행하다 implies the whole trip, not a single going. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: (1) saying just 가다 ('I went to Busan' = 부산에 갔어요) when you mean a vacation — add 여행; (2) attaching 에 to 여행하다 (제주도에 여행해요) — for the verb 여행하다 the place is the object (제주도를 여행해요), while with 가다 you use 으로/에. As a 하다 verb, negate inside: 여행 안 해요.

Wrong particle with the verb: '제주도에 여행해요' is off — 여행하다 takes the place as object: 제주도를 여행해요. (With 가다 it's 제주도로/에 여행 가요.)
Saying 안 여행해요. Inside the 하다 verb: 여행 안 해요 — though 여행 안 가요 ('not going on a trip') is what Koreans more naturally say.

usage: Space + 을/를 + 청소하다; cleaning a whole area.
집/방/화장실을 청소하다 — typical spaces, not single objects.
I run the vacuum (lit. spin the cleaner).
청소기 = vacuum; the idiom is 청소기를 돌리다, part of cleaning.
I did a big / deep clean.
대청소 (great-cleaning) = spring clean; 청소 is a productive noun.
examples: 방 좀 청소해!
Clean your room, would you!
Casual command with 좀 softening (or nagging) the order.
손님이 오니까 청소해야 해요.
Guests are coming, so I have to clean.
-니까 (since) gives the reason; 청소해야 하다 = must clean.
주말마다 같이 집을 청소해요.
We clean the house together every weekend.
주말마다 (every weekend) + 청소하다 for a shared routine.
nuance: 청소하다 is 한자 淸掃 (淸 'clear, pure' + 掃 'sweep') + 하다 — literally 'sweep clean,' i.e. tidy up a room or space. The boundary with neighboring verbs is what trips learners: 씻다 = wash a body or food with water (손을 씻다, 과일을 씻다); 닦다 = wipe, scrub a surface, or polish (창문을 닦다, 이를 닦다 = brush teeth); 치우다 = clear away / put things in order (책상을 치우다). 청소하다 is the umbrella 'clean a space,' so you 청소하다 a room but 닦다 the table inside it and 씻다 your hands afterward. The English-speaker pitfall is using one English 'clean' for all of these — saying 방을 씻어요 (washing the room with water) is unintentionally literal and odd; rooms are 청소해요. Natural partners: 방·집·화장실을 청소하다, 청소기를 돌리다, 대청소. As a 하다 verb the negative goes inside: 청소 안 해요, 청소 못 해요.

mistakes: Using 씻다 (wash with water) for tidying a room: '방을 씻어요' literally means hosing the room down. A room is 방을 청소해요.
Using 청소하다 for wiping one surface or brushing teeth: the table is 닦아요, teeth are 이를 닦아요, not 청소해요. 청소하다 is for whole spaces.

usage: The natural form: 노래를 부르다 (sing a song), preferred over bare 노래하다.
I'm a good singer (lit. I do songs well).
노래(를) 잘하다 = be good at singing; a very common compliment.
노래방 (song-room) = the karaoke room where Koreans actually sing.
Counter 곡 for songs; 노래 한 곡 하다 = perform a number.
examples: 노래 불러 줘.
Sing for me.
Casual 불러 줘; Koreans say 노래(를) 부르다, not 노래하다, for singing a specific song.
우리 같이 노래할까요?
Shall we sing together?
노래할까요? proposes singing as a shared activity.
저는 사람 앞에서 노래 못 해요.
I can't sing in front of people.
Negative ability 노래 못 하다, with 못 inside the 하다 verb.
nuance: 노래하다 joins the native noun 노래 'a song' with 하다 to mean 'to sing,' but here's the catch that surprises learners: Koreans usually prefer 노래(를) 부르다 ('call out a song') for the act of singing, especially singing a particular song — 노래를 불러 주세요 sounds far more natural than 노래해 주세요. Bare 노래하다 leans poetic or general ('the birds are singing'), while 노래를 부르다 is the everyday choice at a 노래방 (karaoke room). For 'I'm a good singer,' the set phrase is 노래를 잘하다 (do songs well). Don't confuse it with 부르다 used alone, which also means 'to call (someone)' — context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'sing' one-to-one onto 노래하다 and never reaching for 부르다, which is what natives actually say. As a 하다 verb, the negative splits inside: 노래 안 해요, 노래 못 해요. Note 부르다 itself is a 르 irregular (불러요), separate from 노래하다's regular 하다 conjugation.

usage: 음악에 맞춰 (in time with the music) + 춤추다.
Split form 춤을 추다 lets you add 잘 (well); very natural.
The noun 춤 also pairs with 배우다 (learn) — 춤을 배우다.
춤 실력 (dance ability) — 춤 as a noun in a compliment.
examples: 같이 춤출래?
Wanna dance together?
Casual invitation with -ㄹ래? — friendly, low-pressure.
파티에서 친구들이랑 춤추고 싶어요.
I want to dance with friends at the party.
친구들이랑 (casual 'with friends') + 춤추고 싶다.
사람이 많으면 춤 못 춰요.
I can't dance when there are a lot of people.
Negative ability; 춤 못 춰요 splits the noun off — note the 춰 contraction.
nuance: 춤추다 is a fused noun+verb: the noun 춤 'a dance' plus the native verb 추다 'to dance, perform (a dance).' Because 추다 already means 'dance,' the headword often un-fuses into 춤을 추다, especially when you add a modifier — 춤을 잘 추다 (dance well), 춤을 배우다 (learn to dance), 춤 실력 (dancing ability). The big pitfall: there is no verb 춤하다 — dancing does NOT take 하다 the way 노래(하다) or 운동(하다) do, because 추다 is its dedicated verb; saying 춤해요 is a classic beginner slip. Conjugation: the stem 추 + -어 contracts to 춰 (춰요, 춤췄어요, 춤출 거예요), and in the negative the noun separates so 안/못 land before the verb: 춤 안 춰요, 춤 못 춰요. Compare 노래하다, where the parallel and equally common form is 노래를 부르다 — both 'dance' and 'sing' prefer the noun + dedicated-verb construction over a plain 하다 verb.
